problems.nature: rare and sophisticated network intrusion attacks focusing on Remote-to-Local (R2L) and User-to-Root (U2R) privilege escalation
problems.description: This cybersecurity problem involves detecting rare and highly imbalanced network intrusion events where attackers attempt to gain unauthorized local access from remote locations (R2L) or escalate privileges from user-level to root-level access (U2R). The dataset focuses exclusively on these critical and challenging attack types alongside normal network traffic, reflecting real-world scenarios where such attacks are sparse but highly impactful. The attacks are characterized by subtle anomalies in network connection features, host behavior, and traffic patterns, making detection difficult. The data includes detailed connection metadata such as protocol, service, flags, byte counts, login attempts, and various error rates, which collectively provide a comprehensive view of network activity for anomaly detection.
problems.attack_vector: exploitation of network services and protocols to gain unauthorized access and escalate privileges remotely, often through brute force, exploitation of vulnerabilities, or malicious payload delivery
problems.asset_targeted: networked computing systems and servers, particularly their authentication mechanisms, user privilege levels, and critical system resources
problems.impact_level: high severity due to the potential for unauthorized root access and control over critical systems, enabling data breaches, system compromise, and further lateral movement within networks

indicators_of_compromise: anomalous service usage (e.g., ftp_data, http with suspicious flags)
high counts of connections to same host/service in short time (count, srv_count)
abnormal error rates (serror_rate, rerror_rate, srv_serror_rate, srv_rerror_rate)
unusual file creation or access operations (num_file_creations, num_access_files)
flags indicating successful or rejected connections (flag = SF or REJ)
attack_patterns: short or zero duration connections with suspicious service usage
zero or low src_bytes but high dst_bytes indicating data exfiltration
successful login followed by root shell or file access
low error rates but high connection counts to specific hosts/services
presence of hot indicators and privilege escalation flags
rare but distinct combinations of network and host features signaling R2L or U2R
normal_patterns: consistent protocol usage (tcp, udp) with expected service patterns
no failed login attempts and no privilege escalation indicators
stable connection counts with low error rates
flags predominantly indicating normal connection status (SF)
absence of hot indicators or suspicious file operations

risk_reduction: implement multi-factor authentication and strict access controls to mitigate R2L attacks
deploy host-based intrusion detection systems to monitor privilege escalation attempts
utilize anomaly detection models trained on imbalanced datasets focusing on rare events
continuous monitoring of network traffic and connection metadata for early detection
apply network segmentation and least privilege principles to limit attack surface
regular patching and vulnerability management to reduce exploitation vectors
employ behavior-based detection leveraging host and network features
use threshold-based alerts on indicators like failed logins, root shell access, and unusual service usage
problems.data_context_notes: The detailed data_info.yaml provided comprehensive metadata on the dataset's focus on rare R2L and U2R attacks, schema definitions, and feature descriptions, enabling precise identification of relevant indicators and attack patterns. The inclusion of difficulty levels and multi-class labels enhanced understanding of detection challenges. Sample data exemplified real-world rare attack characteristics and benign traffic, grounding the problem definition in practical observations. This rich context allowed for a nuanced and accurate cybersecurity problem formulation tailored to rare event detection in network intrusion scenarios.

original_data_info.data_description:
A curated subset of the NSL-KDD network intrusion detection dataset focusing exclusively 
on rare attack types (R2L and U2R) along with normal network traffic. This dataset contains 
only attacks that appear in both training and testing sets, making it ideal for rare event 
detection, imbalanced learning research, and cybersecurity anomaly detection studies. 
The dataset includes Remote-to-Local (R2L) attacks where attackers gain unauthorized local 
access from remote locations, and User-to-Root (U2R) attacks where attackers escalate 
privileges from user-level to root access. These represent the most critical and challenging 
attack types to detect in network security, with severe class imbalance reflecting 
real-world cybersecurity scenarios.
original_data_info.data_schema:
duration: Length of the network connection in seconds
protocol_type: Type of network protocol used (tcp, udp, icmp)
service: Network service used on the destination (http, ftp, smtp, etc.)
flag: Status of the connection (SF=normal, REJ=rejected, etc.)
src_bytes: Number of data bytes sent from source to destination
dst_bytes: Number of data bytes sent from destination to source
land: Binary indicator if connection is from/to the same host/port
wrong_fragment: Number of wrong fragments in the connection
urgent: Number of urgent packets in the connection
hot: Number of hot indicators (accessing system directories, creating programs, etc.)
num_failed_logins: Number of failed login attempts
logged_in: Binary indicator if successfully logged in
num_compromised: Number of compromised conditions
root_shell: Binary indicator if root shell was obtained
su_attempted: Binary indicator if su root command attempted
num_root: Number of root accesses
num_file_creations: Number of file creation operations
num_shells: Number of shell prompts
num_access_files: Number of operations on access control files
num_outbound_cmds: Number of outbound commands in an ftp session
is_host_login: Binary indicator if the login belongs to the host list
is_guest_login: Binary indicator if the login is a guest login
count: Number of connections to the same host as the current connection in the past 2 seconds
srv_count: Number of connections to the same service as the current connection in the past 2 seconds
serror_rate: Percentage of connections that have SYN errors
srv_serror_rate: Percentage of connections to the same service that have SYN errors
rerror_rate: Percentage of connections that have REJ errors
srv_rerror_rate: Percentage of connections to the same service that have REJ errors
same_srv_rate: Percentage of connections to the same service
diff_srv_rate: Percentage of connections to different services
srv_diff_host_rate: Percentage of connections to different hosts
dst_host_count: Number of connections having the same destination host
dst_host_srv_count: Number of connections having the same destination host and using the same service
dst_host_same_srv_rate: Percentage of connections having the same destination host and using the same service
dst_host_diff_srv_rate: Percentage of different services on the current host
dst_host_same_src_port_rate: Percentage of connections to the current host having the same src port
dst_host_srv_diff_host_rate: Percentage of connections to the same service coming from different hosts
dst_host_serror_rate: Percentage of connections to the current host that have an S0 error
dst_host_srv_serror_rate: Percentage of connections to the current host and specified service that have an S0 error
dst_host_rerror_rate: Percentage of connections to the current host that have an RST error
dst_host_srv_rerror_rate: Percentage of connections to the current host and specified service that have an RST error
attack_type: Original attack type name (normal, guess_passwd, warezclient, etc.)
difficulty_level: Difficulty level of detecting this particular record (1-21, higher means harder to detect)
label: Binary classification label (0=normal traffic, 1=malicious attack)
sub_label: Multi-class label specifying attack category (normal, r2l, u2r)
